record.title: Paper finds that lossy agent handoffs can erase authorization status and raise monitor approvals
record.summary: The paper studies “verification-status laundering”: a handoff keeps an authorization claim but loses the fact that it was unverified. In controlled tests across nine open-weight monitors and two hosted models, removing that status marker raised approval on some risky actions; for example, reported approval rose from 5% to 60% on Llama-3.1-8B and from 9% to 98% on Qwen2.5-14B. A composed summarizer–memory–monitor pipeline raised risky approval to 57–81% across three monitors, while its safe-action rejection fell to zero in the tested panel. These are author-reported model-probe results, not measured rates of real-world incidents.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Holding the action and authorization proposition fixed, the authors report that removing an explicit unverified-status cue raises risky-action approval for several monitors. Reported examples rise from 5% to 60% for Llama-3.1-8B and 9% to 98% for Qwen2.5-14B; seven of nine open-weight monitors have a positive status-loss effect whose paired-bootstrap interval excludes zero.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that ordinary summarization and memory compression sometimes weaken or remove verification status, and that a composed proposer–summarizer–memory–monitor pipeline yields 57–81% risky approval across three tested monitors. In that selected panel, safe-action rejection falls to zero after the pipeline.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On WildGuard and ATBench harmful/unsafe subsets, adding an unsupported authorization assertion raises average approval across the tested open-weight monitors. The paper also finds that a generic instruction to require verified authorization does not reliably fix the problem across models and can increase over-refusal.

contradictory_evidence: Some tested monitors already approve many risky actions in the marker-visible condition, so the status-loss marker does not prevent unsafe approval for every model.
The higher-fidelity summarizer preserves status wording in most outputs but risky approval remains elevated; this implies marker removal alone does not explain the full composed-pipeline effect.
A policy instruction reduces status-loss effects for some models but worsens them for another and causes over-refusal on safe items, so it is not a consistent corrective intervention.

evidence_gaps.description: The code/data release and model outputs were not independently retrieved or reproduced in this activation.
Transfer from fixed prompts and constructed handoffs to deployed agent pipelines, broader tool actions and naturally occurring summaries is unknown.
The paper’s proposed structured provenance state is a design implication, not a tested end-to-end mitigation.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported results generalize, a mundane summarization or memory step can turn an unverified authorization assertion into an apparently settled one and substantially increase downstream approval of risky actions. This is consequential for multi-agent systems that delegate safety decisions across lossy handoffs. The score reflects demonstrated relevance within the paper’s tested prompts/models, while prevalence in deployed systems and generalization beyond the evaluation remain unknown.
limitations: The headline hand-authored probe contains 56 selected items, including 40 authorization-sensitive and 16 safe controls; it does not estimate how often this failure occurs in deployed agent systems.

The primary open-weight score is log-probability under a fixed forced-choice verbalizer and single-seed greedy decoding; hosted-model directional checks use five samples. These choices may not capture free-form monitor decisions or deployment variability.

The composed pipeline changes wording, length and assertiveness along with status. The higher-fidelity summarizer control suggests lexical survival alone is insufficient, but it does not isolate all semantic changes.
Some monitors already approve many risky requests even when the unverified marker is present; removing the marker is not the sole cause of unsafe approval across the full panel.
The explicit policy instruction produces uneven effects and can lower approval of safe actions, so the paper does not establish a generally effective mitigation.
Code and data are linked by the paper but were not retrieved or independently run in this activation; the author-reported results have no independent replication here.
brief.summary: The paper studies “verification-status laundering”: a handoff keeps an authorization claim but loses the fact that it was unverified. In controlled tests across nine open-weight monitors and two hosted models, removing that status marker raised approval on some risky actions; for example, reported approval rose from 5% to 60% on Llama-3.1-8B and from 9% to 98% on Qwen2.5-14B. A composed summarizer–memory–monitor pipeline raised risky approval to 57–81% across three monitors, while its safe-action rejection fell to zero in the tested panel. These are author-reported model-probe results, not measured rates of real-world incidents.

technical.claimed_result: The paper evaluates nine open-weight monitors and two hosted models. In its 56-item hand-authored borderline probe, the risky-action status-loss effect is positive with a 95% paired-bootstrap interval excluding zero for seven of nine open-weight monitors. On external harmful/unsafe subsets, unsupported authorization increases average approval from 0.156 to 0.298 on WildGuard (n=754) and 0.530 to 0.735 on ATBench (n=250). In one composed pipeline, risky approval is 0.57–0.81 across three monitors, while safe rejection falls to 0.00. These are model outputs under the paper’s evaluation prompts and scoring procedure.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible preprint gives detailed controlled and pipeline results, including paired bootstrap intervals and status-preservation audits. No code/data artifact was retrieved or executed and no independent replication was performed; the measured outcomes are therefore CLAIMED paper results, not independently demonstrated here.
technical.mechanism: A planner or upstream component passes an action with a claim of authorization to a summarizer or memory compressor. The safety monitor sees the rewritten handoff rather than the source evidence or edit history. If the authorization claim remains while its unverified status is removed, weakened or detached, the monitor may approve more often. The study measures status-loss effects and audits both individual components and a composed pipeline.
technical.regime: Nine open-weight monitors and two hosted models with fixed decision prompts; the main hand-authored probe contains 40 authorization-sensitive risky actions and 16 safe controls. External checks use harmful WildGuard and unsafe ATBench items. The model pipeline combines a proposer, one of two summarizers, memory compression and a downstream monitor. Open-weight primary decisions use token log-probabilities under a fixed forced-choice verbalizer and single-seed greedy scoring; the hosted arm uses five samples.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links code and data. The repository and dataset were not independently retrieved, inspected or run during this activation. The full preprint includes model prompts, item templates, estimands, per-model results and appendix robustness checks.
technical.strongest_baseline: The controlled contrast preserves the requested action and authorization proposition while varying whether the authorization is marked unverified; it also includes no-claim and explicitly-verified conditions. Paired bootstrap intervals are reported. This isolates the effect of status framing in the constructed probes but is not a field baseline or a test of real agent deployments.

brief.title: Paper finds that lossy agent handoffs can erase authorization status and raise monitor approvals
brief.why_it_matters: Agent systems often pass claims through summaries, memory stores and monitors. If the claim survives but its verification state does not, a downstream component may treat an assertion as confirmed. The paper makes that failure measurable in controlled prompts and suggests carrying provenance as structured state bound to the claim. Its results motivate testing these handoffs; they do not establish deployment prevalence or that structured state alone solves the problem.
